title: 2 Corinthians
tagline: Paul's most personal letter: weakness, comfort, reconciliation, and a ministry questioned.
author: Paul
authorNote: The letter names Paul as author (1:1), with Timothy beside him, and almost no scholar doubts that. The main debate is about the letter's shape: the tone changes sharply at chapter 10, and some scholars think chapters 10 to 13 were a separate letter (perhaps the "letter of tears" or a later one) joined to chapters 1 to 9, while others think it is one letter written after a change of mood. Some also wonder whether chapters 8 and 9, or 6:14-7:1, were originally separate. The letter itself shows that Paul wrote several letters to Corinth (1 Corinthians 5:9; 2 Corinthians 2:3-4, 7:8).
audience: The church in Corinth, with the believers throughout Achaia
audienceNote: The same church as 1 Corinthians, after a painful visit and a tense exchange of letters. Some in Corinth had been won over by outside teachers whom Paul sarcastically calls "super-apostles" (11:5), and who questioned Paul's authority, his speaking, and his refusal to take pay. Many in the church seem to have repented after Titus's visit (7:6-16), but a minority were still opposed.
setting: Macedonia, probably autumn about AD 55 or 56, after Paul left Ephesus
settingNote: After 1 Corinthians, Paul visited Corinth in a painful visit, sent a severe letter, and then left Ephesus for Troas and Macedonia, anxious to hear from Titus. Titus met him with good news (7:5-7), and Paul wrote from Macedonia, planning to come to Corinth a third time (12:14; 13:1). The order of events is pieced together from hints in the letter, and some details are uncertain.
genreNote: A personal letter, at times a defense, at times a heartfelt appeal. Paul moves among thanksgiving, explanation, a teaching about the new covenant, a fundraising appeal, and, at the end, an ironic "fool's speech" in which he boasts only of his weaknesses.
bigIdea: God comforts and reconciles through weakness: the Christ who was crucified in weakness works through a servant who carries the treasure in a clay jar, so that the power is clearly God's.
mapTitle: Map: Troas, Macedonia, Corinth, and Jerusalem
mapSummary: Paul moves from Ephesus to Troas and on to Macedonia, waiting for news from Corinth, and turns his thoughts to Jerusalem and the collection.
